title: Rip Van Winkle
description: Washington Irving's 1819 tale of a good-natured, idle villager who drinks with ghostly Dutch sailors in the Catskills, sleeps twenty years, and walks home into a new country.

cover.alt: Ghostly Dutchmen playing ninepins in the mountains
cover.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: One afternoon in the mountains and a whole revolution is gone. Rip wakes with a grey beard to a country that has changed its name.

images.alt: Rip wakes up old, his gun rusted
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Nobody in the village knows him, so he no longer knows himself. Identity turns out to be something the neighbours hold for you.

images.alt: The crowd at the new hotel eyes Rip
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The laziest man in the village comes out best: his scolding wife is dead, he is free of work, and he becomes its most respected storyteller.

images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Irving's hero is lovable precisely because he is useless. He will do anyone's work but his own.
chunks.source_quote: The great error in Rip’s composition was an insuperable aversion to all kinds of profitable labour.

images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The ghostly crew plays a cheerful game in total silence, and the silence is what frightens Rip.
chunks.source_quote: On a level spot in the centre was a company of odd-looking personages playing at ninepins.

images.alt: Ghostly Dutchmen playing ninepins in the mountains
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Faced with his own son, a lazy copy of himself leaning on a tree, Rip loses hold of who he is.
chunks.source_quote: “God knows!” exclaimed he, at his wit’s end; “I’m not myself--I’m somebody else--that’s me yonder

images.alt: The villagers stare at the stranger
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The inn sign is the same face with a new coat: King George has become General Washington. Irving's joke is that a revolution can look like a change of paint.
chunks.source_quote: He recognised on the sign, however, the ruby face of King George, under which he had smoked so many a peaceful pipe; but even this was singularly metamorphosed.

images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Irving notes how Rip's tale shifts each time he tells it until it hardens into the version everyone knows: a little lesson in how legends are made.
chunks.source_quote: He was observed, at first, to vary on some points every time he told it

images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Alice tells the Caterpillar "I'm not myself, you see"; Rip tells a crowd "I'm not myself--I'm somebody else". Both stories put a person in front of strangers who demand to know who they are, at the moment the person has lost the answer.

images.alt: Rip finds his house in ruins
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: In Shards: Echo, Denis leaves for seventy light-years rather than live in a world that talks only of war. Rip makes the same escape by accident and comes back to find the war over. Both stories ask what happens to a person when the history they belonged to goes on without them.

images.alt: Children follow Rip, pointing at his beard
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Irving borrowed the plot from German folk tales of a goatherd who sleeps for years after watching a ghostly game of ninepins, and moved it to the Hudson Valley. The story appeared in The Sketch Book in 1819 and helped give the young United States a folklore of its own.

images.alt: The Catskills, a region full of fable
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text:
Rip Van Winkle is a comedy about missing everything. The American Revolution, the founding of a nation, the great political awakening of his neighbours: Rip sleeps through all of it and wakes to a man haranguing the tavern about "rights of citizens--elections--members of congress", which to him is "a perfect Babylonish jargon". Irving clearly finds the new politics a little absurd, and the old Dutch village a little dear.

But the story's emotional center is not politics. It is the terror of returning to a home where nobody recognises you, and the relief of being recognised by a daughter. Rip's twenty years are every exile's twenty years compressed into a night. That is why the tale outlived its era: anyone who has come back after a long absence, from prison, war, illness or emigration, has stood in the street like Rip, looking for a face they know.

images.alt: The Kaatskill mountains above the village
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.
